sources.fact: Goosebumps (piloerection) are an involuntary reaction of the sympathetic nervous system: tiny muscles contract at the base of each hair follicle. Triggers: sudden cold, fear, shock, anger or excitement, and frisson from music or movies. In animals it makes them appear larger to predators (cats puffing up). In humans they don't appear to have much purpose beyond helping conserve heat.

Arrector pili muscles pull hair upright. For animals with thick fur this helps keep them warm, but it doesn't do so for people, who have too little hair to retain warmth. In mice, these muscles and their nerves activate hair follicle stem cells and can lead to new hair growth (Cell, 2020).

post.instagram_caption:
Goosebumps are your body reaching for fur you don't have 🐈

When you're cold, tiny muscles at the base of each hair contract and pull the hair upright. In animals with thick fur that fluffed coat helps keep them warm, and a puffed up cat also looks bigger to predators.

Humans have too little hair for it to keep us warm, yet it still happens with cold, fear, excitement and even music. In mice, scientists found the same system helps hair grow back.

Sources: Cleveland Clinic, NIH.
